requested.title: baseContentType() ignores comma-delimited Content-Type values, letting an upstream bypass the inline-safe allowlist and render HTML/SVG at the app origin
SSRF guard fails open on both switches: an empty allowedHosts array disables the allowlist, and an absent blockPrivateNetworks skips all address validation and pinning
escapeHtmlAttr() does not escape single quotes, so it is unsafe for the single-quoted and unquoted attribute contexts its name implies it covers
headResponse() buffers the entire response body on HEAD, hanging forever on non-SSE streams and heap-allocating whole files GET would stream

```json
[
  {
    "findingId": "F1",
    "verdict": "true-positive",
    "adjustedSeverity": "HIGH",
    "reasoning": "I traced the whole chain and every link holds. `baseContentType()` splits only on `;`, so `image/png;x=1, text/html` normalizes to `image/png` and hits `INLINE_SAFE_IMAGE_TYPES`; `safeOriginalContentType()` (imageEndpoint.ts:26-29) then returns `{ contentType: <raw upstream string>, attachment: false }`, and lines 103-114 emit that raw string verbatim with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and **no** `Content-Disposition`. The upstream value is never normalized upstream of that: `fetchImageSource` returns `res.headers.get('content-type')` raw (fetchSource.ts:122), `ImageCache.getOriginal` stores it unmodified (imageCache.ts:288) and `metaFrom` hands it back verbatim, so the poisoned type persists across the SWR disk cache and is re-served under a stable URL. I confirmed there is no byte/format validation on the `original` path — `inputFormats` is enforced only at resize.ts:67, on the variant path — and the image route is registered straight into `bunRoutes` (Mochi.ts:1707), so no `handle` middleware, `filterResponseHeaders`, or CSP ever touches it; the repo's only CSP is `packages/support/src/embedHeaders.ts` (`frame-ancestors`), exactly as the finding states. On the browser side I could not fetch the specs directly (egress denied), but search surfaced two independent confirmations of the parser differential: BlackFan's `content-type-research/XSS.md` catalogs comma-separated Content-Type values as a Chrome+Firefox XSS vector *with `nosniff` set*, and the 'Parse and Parse' research reports `application/json;,text/html` being parsed as `text/html` by Chromium-based browsers and Firefox — precisely the `<allowlisted>;<param>,text/html` shape here, and Chromium's net layer splitting Content-Type on commas is called out there too. Concrete attack: an app proxies an upstream whose Content-Type is attacker-influenced (a user-supplied `src`, which docs/148-images.md:262 explicitly blesses, or a user-uploaded S3/GCS object where the uploader sets the type); the upstream replies `Content-Type: image/png;x=1, text/html` with an HTML+script body; the minted `/_mochi/image/<name>?p=<token>` URL serves it inline at the app origin, and any top-level navigation to that URL (shared link, open-image-in-new-tab) executes attacker script same-origin with cookie access. `image/png;x=1, image/svg+xml` gives scriptable SVG identically. This defeats a named, documented guarantee ('A full-size original that is SVG (or any non-raster type) is served as a download rather than inline') and the control's own doc comment names the exact threat. Tests at imageEndpoint.test.ts:45-64 cover `;` params and case folding but never a comma, and :62 asserts the raw echo. The second call site (dev/emailViewerRoutes.ts:89-98) has the identical defect and additionally sets `Content-Disposition: inline`, though it is dev-only behind `emailViewerEnabled`. Nothing is fixed — the file is unchanged since #158. I keep HIGH: it requires a top-level navigation and a not-fully-trusted upstream, which is why it isn't CRITICAL, but it is a total bypass of a first-party security control in a published npm framework with same-origin script execution as the payoff."
  },
  {
    "findingId": "F2",
    "verdict": "false-positive",
    "reasoning": "Both halves dissolve once the call graph is pinned down. (1) `blockPrivateNetworks === undefined` is unreachable: `resolvePublicUrl` has exactly one non-test caller, `fetchSource.ts:83-86`, which forwards `ResolvedImageOptions`, where the field is typed as a **required** `boolean` (image/types.ts:158) and resolved eagerly as `o.blockPrivateNetworks ?? true` (image/config.ts:100). So no shipped code path can omit it. I also verified `resolvePublicUrl`, `UrlGuardOptions` and `SsrfGuardError` are **not** exported from `packages/mochi/src/index.ts`, so this is not public API and no third-party caller can omit it either — the 'second caller' is hypothetical, and the finding itself concedes this half is latent. (2) The empty-array half is a config footgun, not a vulnerability. No code anywhere in the monorepo produces `allowedHosts: []` (the only in-repo configs are `packages/site` setting `blockPrivateNetworks: false` with hardcoded sources, and test fixtures with real host lists); `allowedHosts` is explicitly optional in the guard's own contract and the published default is documented as 'any public host' (docs/148-images.md:250), so `[]` → no allowlist is consistent with absent rather than a reversal of a configured control. Critically, even with the allowlist inert, `blockPrivateNetworks` still defaults to `true`, so loopback/RFC1918/link-local/169.254.169.254/ULA/NAT64/6to4/teredo are all still rejected and every redirect hop is re-validated (fetchSource.ts:80-110) — the residual exposure is 'fetch arbitrary *public* URLs', which is exactly the framework's documented out-of-the-box posture. There is no attacker-controlled input that can empty a configured allowlist; reaching the described state requires an operator to write `[]` or a computed expression that evaluates to it. I agree the defensive changes are worth making (treat a present-but-empty array as deny-all, use `!== false` for the address checks, log once at boot when either control is off), and I note the finding correctly ruled out the rest of the file (the `localhost.` trailing-dot gap is backstopped by DNS resolution, `hostMatches` requires a label before a wildcard suffix, WHATWG URL punycodes IDNs and normalizes octal/hex/decimal IPv4 literals before `isIP()`). But as written there is no exploitable path, so MEDIUM SSRF overstates it; if it were kept at all it belongs at BUG/hardening severity."
  },
  {
    "findingId": "F3",
    "verdict": "false-positive",
    "reasoning": "The technical claim about the function is accurate — `ATTR_REPLACEMENTS` covers only `& \" < >`, so `'`, backtick, space and `=` pass through and the function would not protect a single-quoted or unquoted attribute. But I enumerated every call site in the monorepo and none of them is in such a context. Mochi.ts:1662 is ` props=\"${escapeHtmlAttr(serializedProps)}\"`; Mochi.ts:1686 is `<template ${BOOTSTRAP_MARKER_ATTR}=\"${escapeHtmlAttr(bootstrapUrl)}\">`; islandFailureStub.ts:38/42 are `data-component=\"…\"` and `data-message=\"…\"` — all double-quoted, where a literal `'` is inert. The remaining two uses (packages/site/src/lib/highlight.server.ts:37 and the example in docs/140-utility-helpers.md:97) put the value in `<code>` **text content**, where escaping `&`, `<` and `>` is exactly sufficient and quotes are irrelevant. I found no single-quoted or unquoted attribute assembly anywhere in `packages/site`, `demos`, `support`, the web components, or generated module source, and nothing that drops the output into a `<script>` or other non-HTML context. The contract is also stated rather than merely implied: the docstring reads 'Escape a string for embedding in a **double-quoted** HTML attribute', and the public docs page enumerates precisely the four characters replaced, so a reader is told what is and is not covered. That leaves a real but theoretical footgun for third-party app authors who ignore the stated scope — a defense-in-depth API-hardening item, not a vulnerability with an attack path in this codebase, and the finding's own text concedes 'not currently exploitable inside the repo' (consistent with its self-assessed low confidence). The suggested fix is cheap and risk-free (adding `'` and backtick preserves the `getAttribute()` round-trip because `&` is replaced first) and I'd endorse making it plus tightening the doc wording — but as a security finding it does not survive verification."
  },

    "findingId": "F4",
    "verdict": "true-positive",
    "adjustedSeverity": "BUG",
    "reasoning": "Verified as described. `headResponse` (utils/index.ts:266-274) drains `await res.arrayBuffer()` for any body whose Content-Type does not contain `text/event-stream`, and `withHead` applies it to every `Mochi.api()` route (Mochi.ts:1257), both page arms (1182/1192), the island endpoint (1559), the image endpoint (1707) and the local-asset route (1727), while the catch-all `fetch` handler calls `headResponse(response)` directly on HEAD (1932). Claim (1) holds: an ordinary streaming non-SSE route (NDJSON, a log tail, `application/octet-stream`, a proxied token stream) answers HEAD by awaiting a body that never ends — the promise never settles, the handler never returns, and the buffer grows for the life of the process. Nothing cancels it in-process: the stream is one the handler owns, so a client disconnect does not cancel it, and the app never opted into HEAD at all (the object arm even synthesizes a `HEAD` entry so Bun does not 405). One correction to the finding's rationale: `api: { timeout: false }` in KIND_POLICY means `server.timeout(req, 0)` — which *disables* the idle timeout — is **not** called, so api requests keep Bun's default ~10s idle timeout rather than having none. That only closes the socket and aborts `req.signal`, though; it does not cancel the already-running `arrayBuffer()` drain, so the unbounded-growth conclusion survives even though the stated reason is inverted. Claim (2) holds: `serveDiskAsset` returns `new Response(Bun.file(path))` (serveDiskAsset.ts:22), reached both via `withHead(createLocalAssetHandler(...))` at 1727 and via the catch-all's `diskAsset` branch at 1894 → 1932, so HEAD reads a whole font/CSS/image file into the heap solely to compute a length `BunFile` already exposes as `file.size`. The correct pattern is already in the tree — `Mochi.file`'s HEAD arm at Mochi.ts:1492-1493 uses `file.size` — and `withHead`'s own doc comment ('`Response` and `BunFile` pass through untouched') is true only of a BunFile *route value*, not of a handler returning `new Response(file)`, so it actively misleads here. Claim (3) is a genuine undocumented constraint, latent only because index.ts:291 skips bare `Response`/`Blob` route values. The author's own test at index.test.ts:267-277 ('A never-ending stream: if headResponse buffered it, this test would hang') shows the hazard was understood and the guard was simply keyed on one content type. BUG is the right severity: it is reachable by an unauthenticated HEAD, but the unbounded-hang half requires the app to expose a streaming route, and the disk-asset half is bounded by file size (memory amplification rather than a true leak). The recommended fix — branch on what the body is (absent / BunFile-Blob `.size` / existing Content-Length / else omit Content-Length and `res.body.cancel()`) — is correct and mirrors the existing `Mochi.file` code."
  }
]
```

**Summary:** F1 and F4 confirmed; F2 and F3 are hardening items with no attack path.

- **F1 (HIGH, true-positive)** — Fully verified end to end: `;`-only splitting lets `image/png;x=1, text/html` pass the inline-safe allowlist, the raw upstream header is echoed with no `Content-Disposition`, the poisoned type is cached, no CSP or middleware covers the image route, and the `original` path does no format validation. Browser-side last-wins comma parsing is corroborated by BlackFan's Content-Type research (Chrome+Firefox, `nosniff` present) and the "Parse and Parse" write-up's `application/json;,text/html` → `text/html` result. Breaks a documented guarantee; same bug in the dev email viewer.
- **F4 (BUG, true-positive)** — Confirmed both the infinite-stream hang and the whole-file heap read, plus the undocumented body-consumption contract. One correction: `api: { timeout: false }` actually *keeps* Bun's ~10s idle timeout rather than removing it — but that only closes the socket, so the leak conclusion stands. The right fix already exists in-tree at `Mochi.file`'s HEAD arm.
- **F2 (false-positive)** — `resolvePublicUrl` has one internal caller that always passes a resolved `boolean` (`?? true`), and it isn't a public export, so the `undefined` branch is unreachable. The `allowedHosts: []` half needs an operator misconfiguration no repo code produces, and `blockPrivateNetworks` still blocks all private ranges regardless. Worth hardening, not a MEDIUM SSRF.
- **F3 (false-positive)** — Every call site is a double-quoted attribute or `<code>` text content; the docstring and public docs both scope the function explicitly. Cheap fix worth taking, but no attack path.

Sources for the browser-behavior verification: [BlackFan content-type-research XSS.md](https://github.com/BlackFan/content-type-research/blob/master/XSS.md), [Parse and Parse: MIME Validation Bypass to XSS via Parser Differential](https://lab.ctbb.show/research/parse-and-parse-mime-validation-bypass-to-xss-via-parser-differential), [HackerNotes Ep. 160](https://blog.criticalthinkingpodcast.io/p/hackernotes-ep-160-cloudflare-zero-days-mail-unsubscribing-for-xss), [Chromium net/http/http_util.h](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/net/http/http_util.h), [Chromium http_response_headers.cc](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/dad8d98fc2234f735336be261f2a7eebc22eb2c4/net/http/http_response_headers.cc), [Blink http_parsers.cc](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/791c8335079bbe7abe7a1b7b6251317ec62b2563/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/network/http_parsers.cc), [MDN X-Content-Type-Options](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/X-Content-Type-Options).

Note: I could not fetch the WHATWG mimesniff/Fetch specs or the Chromium source directly — egress to those hosts was denied by the sandbox proxy (and the `web-fetch` agent's WebFetch was denied in don't-ask mode), so F1's browser-parsing step rests on search-surfaced secondary sources rather than primary spec text. That's the one place my F1 confidence is secondhand; the code-path analysis itself is first-hand and complete.
